This doesn't answer your question, but you may be interested in tachyons.

They have yet to be observed, so they may not actually exist, but they travel faster than light, so they "experience" time backwards from our reference frame.

You can check out more on Tachyon particles here.

Although they have yet to be observed it is hypothesized that they must exist because of two complimentary particles known as luxons and bradyons, which move at the speed of light and slower than the speed of light, respectively. So their existence would satisfy our human need of symmetry. They would also fit quite nicely into String Theory, but there existence would mess with known laws of Special Relativity (as string theory already does).

As humans we have a really crappy understanding of what "time" is: time and space are actually one single thing yet due to our evolution and schema building we perceive them to be two entirely separate entities. So keep that in mind.

There is a type of theoretical particle known as a tachyon which has the ability to both move faster than light and move independently of time space. Though such movements violate the rules of causality in special relativity the Lorentz invariance makes room for such an abject to exist by showing that through the underlying symmetry of the theory of special relativity light speed is a non-barrier.

So particles may theoretically exist that "move backwards" through time.

The term 'dark matter' is used to describe the difference between the mass of stars and planets (and other astronomical bodies) that can be determined from their observable gravitational effects and their actual mass calculated from any observable matter which they contain. So dark matter is probably just another type of matter that we do not yet have the technological capacity to properly measure.

Long story short: no, dark matter probably doesn't move backwards through time, if it did all of the stars and planets that we can readily observe would be doing some really crazy stuff up there.
